title: Supreme Court clears the way for border wall construction in Big Bend
excerpt: The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday, Nov. 9, cleared the Trump administration to resume building border barriers in the Big Bend region of West Texas — including parts of Big Bend National Park — while a lawsuit over the project continues.
content:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday, Nov. 9, cleared the Trump administration to resume building border barriers in the Big Bend region of West Texas — including parts of Big Bend National Park — while a lawsuit over the project continues.

In an unsigned five-page ruling, the court lifted an injunction issued in October by U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone of El Paso, who had halted construction. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to publicly dissent. The court said Congress has expressed a “clear preference for expeditious border construction” that outweighs “any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm” claimed by the challengers, and found the administration “exceedingly likely” to win its argument.

The project covers more than 300 miles of barriers and patrol roads across the Big Bend sector, which spans 517 miles — more than a quarter of the entire U.S.-Mexico border. Inside Big Bend National Park, the administration plans 17 miles of noncontiguous vehicle barriers, not the 30-foot pedestrian fencing planned for other areas.

The administration fast-tracked the work by waiving dozens of environmental and conservation laws. Homeland Security Secretaries Kristi Noem and Markwayne Mullin issued the waivers between February and July under a 1996 law that lets the homeland security secretary waive legal requirements in areas designated as having high levels of illegal entry.

The lawsuit was brought by the Center for Biological Diversity, a Big Bend-area river guide, and a group working to preserve a historic adobe church in Ruidosa, Texas, which says the fragile structure is threatened by the construction. Judge Cardone had found that the waivers lacked clear congressional authorization, noting that the Big Bend sector has the lowest number of apprehensions of any Southwest border sector.

Construction had already begun before the court fight: a 47-mile stretch in Hudspeth County started in September, and the administration paused work in August after the project drew bipartisan criticism over its impact on the park's landscape and wildlife. Customs and Border Protection says crews are building about 12 miles of barrier a week, and the agency has awarded five contracts worth more than $6 billion for border security upgrades in Big Bend, including steel fencing, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology.

The ruling is temporary — the case continues in federal court — but it signals that the administration can move quickly on wall construction across Texas border sectors. That includes the Laredo Sector here in Webb County. Webb Watch will track any new construction, contracts or federal announcements affecting this border.
